Text: Although often called a heartbeat, the {{c1::pulse}} is really {{c2::the pressure wave}} sent through the arteries by each heartbeat.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: a heartbeat is the ventricular contraction itself, forcefully ejecting blood into the arteries; the pulse is the traveling wave that surge creates.

Cue: feel the pulse at a pulse point, where a major artery lies near the surface and can be pressed gently against a bone or solid organ.

Text:
Where you palpate the pulse depends on age and responsiveness:

Responsive and older than 1 year → {{c1::radial (at the wrist)}}

Unresponsive and older than 1 year → {{c1::carotid (at the neck)}}

Younger than 1 year → {{c1::brachial (inside of the upper arm)}}
Back Extra:
Why: in infants, the radial and carotid pulses are simply difficult to locate, so the brachial is the site regardless of responsiveness.

Pitfall: never palpate any pulse with your thumb; you may mistake its own strong pulsing for the patient's.

Text: With an infant lying supine, you can reach the brachial pulse by {{c1::elevating the arm over the infant's head::arm maneuver}}.
Back Extra: Cue: infant arms are chubby, so press adjacent fingertips firmly along the brachial artery, which runs parallel to the long axis of the upper arm.

Text: A mother hands you her limp 7-month-old, who does not respond to your voice or touch. Which pulse do you palpate? {{c1::Brachial}}
Back Extra:
Why: under 1 year the radial and carotid pulses are difficult to locate, so the brachial is the site even though she is unresponsive.

Pitfall: "unresponsive → carotid" applies only to patients older than 1 year.

Text:
Your patient is unresponsive:

No palpable carotid pulse → begin {{c1::CPR}}

Pulse present but not breathing → provide {{c1::ventilations}}
Back Extra: Distinguish: the choice applies only to unresponsive patients — never begin CPR or use an AED on a responsive one.

Text: If an AED is available for your unresponsive, pulseless patient, turn it on and follow its {{c1::voice prompts}}, consistent with your {{c1::local protocol}}.
Back Extra: Why: an AED is indicated only for patients already assessed to be unresponsive and pulseless — the pulse check comes before the machine.

Text: An adult who has a pulse but is not breathing gets ventilations at a rate of {{c1::10 to 12}} breaths/min.
Back Extra:
Pitfall: rescue ventilations are for a patient who still HAS a pulse — a pulseless patient gets CPR and the AED instead.

Roster: rescue-ventilation rates — adult 10 to 12; infant or child 12 to 20 breaths/min.

Text: An infant or child who has a pulse but is not breathing gets ventilations at a rate of {{c1::12 to 20}} breaths/min.
Back Extra:
Cue: infants and children share a single range — there is no separate infant band for rescue ventilations.

Roster: rescue-ventilation rates — adult 10 to 12; infant or child 12 to 20 breaths/min.

Text: While ventilating a patient who has a pulse but is not breathing, recheck the pulse every {{c1::2}} minutes to evaluate the effectiveness of your ventilations.
Back Extra: Why: a lost pulse is the failure signal — the moment the patient becomes pulseless, start CPR and apply the AED.

Text: You must never begin CPR or use an AED on a {{c1::responsive::responsive/unresponsive}} patient — apparent pulselessness in that patient is not cardiac arrest.
Back Extra:
Distinguish: an AED is indicated only for patients assessed to be unresponsive AND pulseless — the exact opposite state.

Pitfall: a hard-to-feel pulse alone does not license CPR; responsiveness overrules your fingers.

Text: You find a 58-year-old man collapsed at a gym. He does not respond to painful stimulus, and you cannot palpate a carotid pulse. What do you do first? {{c1::Begin CPR}}
Back Extra:
Why: unresponsive + no palpable carotid pulse = begin CPR; when the AED arrives, turn it on and follow its voice prompts.

Distinguish: had he been responsive, no CPR and no AED — an unfelt pulse in a responsive patient is not cardiac arrest.
